senses: A person who refuses to do something, usually as a protest; for example, one who refuses conscription or vaccination.
ety: From refuse + -nik (suffix denoting a nickname for a person who endorses, exemplifies, or is associated with something, often a particular ideology or preference), a calque of Russian отка́зник (otkáznik), from отка́з (otkáz, “denial, refusal, rejection, repudiation”) + -ник (-nik, suffix forming masculine nouns, usually denoting adherents, etc.).

senses: surface; externality; outside
An adherent of neorealism.
examples: DeSanctis wasn't a neorealist; he was a follower of D'Annunzio, who took calendar-art shots of the sea.

senses: Enfilled with or spread throughout; permeating; pervading.
ety: From Middle English riddil, ridelle (“sieve”). More at riddle.

senses: A person who charters something
examples: When at home, it is usually signed by the owner and the charterer; abroad, by the master and the agent for the charterer.
FI—"Free In." A pricing term indicating that the charterer of a vessel is responsible for the cost of loading goods onto the vessel.

senses: A low screen between columns, especially one that surrounds the choir of a church
A dancing boy in parts of Central Asia.
Being or relating to polymorphic content; developed for multiple formats from the start, instead of being adapted later.
A tuplet of four notes.
A sequence of four elements.
One of a group of four, particularly one of four babies born from the same mother during the same birth.
A cycle for carrying four riders, arranged so that all the riders can assist in the propulsion.
A broad, shallow dish used for drinking, primarily in ritual contexts such as libations.
A circular ornament, resembling a dish, often worked in relief on friezes etc.
The caldera or crater (dish-shaped depression) atop a volcano, especially an extraterrestrial one; also used in the names of extraterrestrial volcanoes which have such a caldera.
examples: What caused the transitions from explosive to effusive volcanism in the Circum-Hellas Volcanic Province generally and during the eruptive lifetimes of individual highland patera volcanoes?
Note that the eroded plains materials to the right of the patera show no signs of individual lava flows.

senses: A person who practices or is interested in sartorialism.
A type of sweet orange, normally seedless.
ety: From Jaffa, an ancient port city in Israel from which the oranges were exported. The sense "impotent male" is a reference to being "seedless"; see seed. The cricketing sense, of a 'sweet ball' (from the bowler's perspective), is a metaphor further reinforced in Australian English where Jaffa is also a trademark for a popular lolly that is red and round.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of Scotch whisky.
examples: Inspired by a Sazerac, here's a superboozy, herbal-Scotchy drink that'll relax your shoulders, loosen your tongue, and clear your mind . . . basically, everything you need a stiff drink to do.

senses: A strong westerly wind, a wind blowing from the west.
A Provençal cold sauce made from cloves of garlic, fresh basil, and olive oil, similar to pesto.
Moment of theoretical suspension of all action.
Moment of theoretical suspension of belief.
ety: Borrowed from Latin epocha or German Epoche, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ). Doublet of epoch. This term was introduced by Husserl and other phenomenologists, although it also seems to be present in Aristotelian philosophy (as the concept did originate with Aristotle).

senses: An abrupt, sharp sound, especially one made by two hard objects colliding repetitively; a sound midway between a click and a clunk.
Anything that causes a clacking noise, such as the clapper of a mill, or a clack valve.
Chatter; prattle.
ety: From Middle English clacken, clakken, claken, from Old English *clacian (“to slap, clap, clack”), from Proto-Germanic *klakōną (“to clap, chirp”). Cognate with Scots clake, claik (“to utter cries", also "to bedaub, sully with a sticky substance”), Dutch klakken (“to clack, crack”), Low German klakken (“to slap on, daub”), Norwegian klakke (“to clack, strike, knock”), Icelandic klaka (“to twitter, chatter, wrangle, dispute”).

senses: A typewriter.
Someone who types; a typist.
examples: I don't trust the human beast, Head, and I don't like crowds. I drink my beer, hit the typer and wait.

senses: Lack of muscle tone; flaccidity or atonia
ety: Borrowed from New Latin atonia, from Ancient Greek ἀτονία (atonía, “languor”), from ἄτονος (átonos, “languid”), from ἀ- (a-, “privative”) + τόνος (tónos, “accent”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”).

senses: A type of ornament worn tightly about the neck.
examples: He was a dog—one of those small, silky, fluffy dogs that look like a fur necklet, until they begin to bark.

senses: To remove something from political influence.
To hold colloquy; to converse.
A Japanese condiment made from fermented bamboo shoots.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese メンマ (menma), blend of ramen + machiku.

senses: The activities of cosmonauts; Soviet/Russian astronautics.
The name of the Latin script letter Ə/ə.
ety: Borrowed from German Schwa, from Hebrew שווא / שְׁוָא (shva, šəwā, “(mark indicating reduction or absence of a vowel)”), borrowed from Classical Syriac ܫ̈ܘܰܝܳܐ (š'wayyā, literally “even, equal”), in Syriac a term for a sign consisting of two vertical dots used to separate parts of a sentence. Doublet of shva.

senses: One who, or that which, eliminates.
A repeated rhythmic pattern used in isorhythm implying a piece cut off.
ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin tālea (1940s), from Latin tālea (“cutting; scion”).

senses: An agogo bell, a bell used in Yoruba and Brazilian music and typically played in pairs
ety: From Portuguese agogô, from Yoruba agogo (“bell”).

senses: A baseball cap.
Close or closest; adjacent.
About to take place; impending.
ety: From Late Latin proximatus, past participle of proximare (“to draw near, approach”), from Latin proximus (“nearest”), superlative of prope (“near”).

senses: To trick (a person) into viewing the image.
To exhibit one's anus to (a person) in a similar manner to the image.
ety: From the name of a now defunct website which first published the image, namely goatse.cx, which used the top-level domain code .cx, reserved for Christmas Island, because an attempt by an English speaker to say the website's full name would result in a string of phonemes sounding like goat sex.

senses: An impure form of tricalcium silicate.
ety: Named by Alfred Elis Törnebohm in 1897 after examining Portland cement through a microscope.

senses: An assignment of the produce and income of a particular district or village to a person or persons, as an annuity
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi जागीर (jāgīr) / Urdu جَاگِیر (jāgīr)), from Classical Persian جَاگِیر (jāgīr, “jagir”), from جَا (jā, “place”) + گِیر (gīr), the present stem of گرفتن (giriftan, “to take”).

senses: A group of three notes of even rhythm played or written where two of those notes would ordinarily be; a form of tuplet.
A constructed gem consisting of a thin slice of natural opal sandwiched between a clear glass or quartz top and a synthetic or stone backing that enhances the colour of the opal.
One of a group of three, particularly
One of a group of three siblings born at the same time to the same mother.
Mounted on a horse.
ety: From Middle English horsed, i-horsed, yhorsed, y-horsed, from Old English horsod, ġehorsod, past participle of Old English horsian, ġehorsian (“to horse”), equivalent to horse + -ed.

senses: A person who makes wisecrack remarks; a smart aleck.
A musical composition in the hotcha style.
A thug (a member of band of assassins in India).
The murder and robbery of groups of travellers in India.
Inflated or swollen.
Gathered up into rounded ridges.
Expanded by the use of steam.
Consisting of a puff; exhaled or produced in puffs.
One who completes something.
